topStories.headline: Film Shoot Honoring Chinatown Divides the Neighborhood It Hopes to Celebrate
topStories.dek: Independent director Pete Lee is wrapping up weeks of on-location shooting for 'High Priestess of Souls,' but merchants say lost parking and street obstructions have cost them business.
topStories.body:
Independent director Pete Lee set out to make something rare: a feature film shot inside San Francisco's Chinatown that treats the neighborhood as a lead character rather than atmosphere. His debut film, 'High Priestess of Souls' — a Hong Kong-style horror comedy starring Joan Chen — began filming on location in October and is scheduled to wrap by the end of November. According to the San Francisco Chronicle's November 14 report on the production, Lee told the paper his mission was to document these places before they change, and that shooting in San Francisco was non-negotiable.

But three weeks into the shoot, the production hit friction with the merchants who live and work there every day. Business owners told the Chronicle that blocked parking spots and partial street obstructions during filming days have deterred customers and made deliveries harder. The tension puts two genuine interests in direct conflict: a filmmaker's desire to preserve Chinatown on screen, and a shopkeeper's need for the foot traffic that keeps a small business alive.

The film is considered a milestone for the neighborhood's representation on screen. It would be, by one account cited in the Chronicle story, the first project both filmed and substantially set in Chinatown since Wayne Wang's 1982 noir 'Chan Is Missing.' Lee received support from the Rainin Foundation for the screenplay in 2019, and the production finally reached cameras this fall with a SAG-AFTRA cast. With filming expected to conclude before December, the production's final weeks are the last window for the two sides to find a workable arrangement.

topStories.headline: Polk Street's Food Pipeline Is Largely Still a Pipeline
topStories.dek: Five food and drink openings were announced this fall along Polk Gulch and Russian Hill — with the holiday season approaching, only one has opened its doors.
topStories.body:
By the first week of October, five food and drink concepts had been announced for the stretch of Polk Street running through Russian Hill and Polk Gulch: a bakery, a bagel shop, a coffee counter, a hand-roll spot, and a single bar. Food writer Jeff Marples checked in on all five and found that just one was open, with the remaining four at various stages of permitting, delayed build-out, or no public timeline at all.

The furthest along in terms of infrastructure was FITNESS SF, which opened its 42,000-square-foot gym at 1600 Jackson Street — just off Polk — on November 1. That adds an anchor at the south end of the corridor, but it is not among the food projects. Of the dining concepts, Freedom Coffee at 1850 Polk has filed for permits but showed no visible build-out as of early October. Bageletto at 2193 Polk had no news since April. The corridor's daytime food lineup, should all five open, would lean heavily toward morning and midday service: the bakery, bagel, coffee, and hand-roll concepts are all pre-dinner operations.

With the holidays now arriving, the window for a 2026 opening is narrowing. Marples noted that the schedule depends entirely on how fast individual build-outs move, and that three storefronts have no firm date at all. Neighbors watching the corridor should expect most of the action to remain on the hill — at hotels and established venues — through at least Thanksgiving.

topStories.headline: Fairmont Kicks Off Holiday Season Saturday with Gingerbread House Lighting and Boys Chorus
topStories.dek: The Nob Hill hotel's annual lighting ceremony — free and open to all — takes place November 21 at 11 a.m., marking the official start of the Fairmont's festive season.
topStories.body:
The Fairmont San Francisco is lighting its life-sized gingerbread house this Saturday, November 21, at 11 a.m. in the hotel's grand lobby at 950 Mason Street. The ceremony, free and open to visitors of all ages, features a live performance by the San Francisco Boys Chorus and special guests from Make-A-Wish Greater Bay Area. The hotel's Rooftop Winter Faire and Carousel Bar also open the same day.

The two-story Victorian-style structure is built each year by the hotel's engineering and culinary teams and traditionally incorporates more than 8,000 gingerbread bricks and roughly 1,900 pounds of candy. Once lit, the display remains in the lobby through December 31 and is free to view throughout the season. The Fairmont's festive programming runs November 21 through the end of the year, making Saturday the opening bell for Nob Hill's holiday calendar — which continues with the Nob Hill Association's annual tree lighting at Huntington Park on November 30.

moreNews.headline: Portsmouth Square Renovation Is Five Months In — and Chinatown Merchants Are Feeling It
moreNews.body: The $73 million renovation of Portsmouth Square — Chinatown's historic public gathering place, often called the neighborhood's 'living room' — has been under active construction since Mayor Daniel Lurie broke ground in June 2026. The pedestrian bridge connecting the square to the Hilton hotel on Kearny Street was demolished in August as the first major milestone. As of August, some merchants near the square reported business dropping by as much as 60 percent since construction began, citing lost parking, noise, and dust as the main factors. The renovation, led by San Francisco Recreation and Parks, is expected to run through fall 2028; the Portsmouth Square Garage at 733 Kearny Street remains open throughout. Residents displaced from the square have been gathering in nearby Chinatown alleyways in the meantime.

moreNews.headline: Demolition Permits Filed for Polk Gulch Mortuary Site, Paving Way for 14-Story Residential Tower
moreNews.body: Demolition permits have been filed for the existing mortuary building at 1123 Sutter Street in Polk Gulch, according to San Francisco YIMBY's permit tracker. The filings represent progress toward a proposed 14-story residential development on the site. No construction start date has been announced publicly.
